title: When the Bell Turns
premise: Lior Thackeray, a pest controller who has spent fifteen years hiding from the thing that once touched his family, is called to the Hollows farmhouse where something leaves fingerprints on the inside of sealed windows. The family's sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, and Lior realizes it is the same entity that marked him as a child. As the harvest moon approaches, the entity begins 'counting' the household, and each name spoken aloud draws its owner closer to being taken. Lior must overcome his lifelong instinct for invisibility, put his own name forward in place of the family's, and burn the recordings before the final count completes—surviving, but forever changed, with the found family he never meant to make.
about_author: L. M. Villalobos grew up in a farming town where the church bell rang at hours no one could explain, an experience that haunts every story they write. They live quietly with two cats and an unshakable habit of checking the locks twice.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A routine pest-control call comes from the remote Hollows farmhouse; Lior almost declines, but the address stirs something he can't name. He arrives to find scratches on the inside of sealed windows. The beat is quiet dread—the past knocking before he's ready to answer.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. He documents handprints too large, too many-jointed, pressed into dust on the inside glass. Teenage daughter Wren watches him work with sharp, suspicious eyes. Emotional beat: professional detachment cracking as recognition flickers—he has seen these prints before, fifteen years ago.

chapters.title: The Hollis Family
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She introduces her exhausted father Marek, gentle stepmother Odile, and mute younger brother Tam, who hasn't spoken since they moved in. Wren resents the stranger poking through their home. Beat: a family fraying under pressure they refuse to name.

chapters.title: Explanations
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. He offers raccoons, settling foundations, anything plausible, and sells them a monitoring setup including sleep recorders. Driving away, he passes the old chapel whose bell hangs motionless yet seems to swing in the mirror. Beat: the comfort of rational lies beginning to fail.

chapters.title: What the Recorders Keep
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, reviewing audio at night. Beneath the family's sleep-breathing, a second voice answers questions nobody asked: 'How many?' 'Four.' Lior freezes—it knows the household size. Beat: cold horror; the invisible life he built is being audited.

chapters.title: Tam Speaks
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Tam wakes the house screaming a number—'five'—though they are four. Odile soothes him while Marek insists it's night terrors. Wren secretly plays back Tam's recorder and hears the second voice say his name. Beat: loyalty to family colliding with the truth she can't unhear.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years Ago
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, interwoven memory. Flashback to his childhood home: the counting voice, his mother answering questions in her sleep, his brother taken after the voice said his name last. Lior survived by never speaking, never being counted. Beat: grief and guilt he buried under routine.

chapters.title: The Bell Turns
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. The derelict chapel bell rings once at 3 a.m.; Marek walks out alone and finds fresh footprints circling the house, always five sets though no one else lives there. Beat: a proud man's denial eroding into fear he won't show his children.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Sleepwalking, Odile answers the voice aloud—'Yes,' 'Soon,' 'Take whoever you like'—and wakes with dirt under her fingernails. Lior confronts her gently; she confesses she's been hearing it for weeks. Beat: shame, complicity, the horror of having bargained without knowing.

chapters.title: Staying Invisible
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. He tries to quit the job, refund the money, drive away—but finds his own name whispered on the recording, added to a list. The thing remembers him. Beat: the devastating realization that invisibility was always a debt coming due.

chapters.title: Rules of the Count
chapters.summary: Lior and Wren's alternating POV. Researching local archives, they learn of disappearances every harvest moon for a century, always households of a certain size, always preceded by the count. The bell marks how many nights remain. Beat: dread sharpening into purpose—an enemy with rules can be fought.

chapters.title: Five Names
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The voice recites five names nightly now: Marek, Odile, Tam, Wren—and Thackeray. Lior admits everything to the family. Marek rages; Odile goes quiet; Tam takes Lior's hand. Beat: the lie of professionalism dies; the seed of found family takes root.

chapters.title: What Odile Promised
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She reveals she answered the voice's early questions hoping it would spare Tam, offering herself. The count accepted her first. Beat: sacrificial love twisted by desperation; the family's anger dissolves into heartbreak.

chapters.title: The Chapel Records
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. In the chapel crypt he finds parish ledgers listing every 'harvest tithe'—names given willingly buy the rest of the household a year. His own mother's handwriting appears in the oldest book. Beat: understanding his survival was purchased, not earned; rage at the economy of sacrifice.

chapters.title: Running
chapters.summary: Marek's POV. Marek loads the family into the truck to flee before the moon. Fifty miles out, the radio counts to five and the road loops back to the Hollows. The farm is a boundary, not a location. Beat: despair—the trap is the land itself.

chapters.title: A Sixth Name
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior realizes the count can be altered: a name freely offered replaces one already listed. He tests it, whispering his own name over the recordings—and the voice pauses, intrigued, then says 'six.' Beat: terrible hope; the mechanism exists, but it may demand more than one name.

chapters.title: The Night Before Harvest
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, rotating. The family spends what may be their last evening together—cooking, telling stories, Tam laughing aloud for the first time in months. Each privately resolves to offer themselves. Beat: bittersweet warmth; love made explicit because time is short.

chapters.title: The Count Begins
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Under the rising harvest moon, the bell tolls and the voice names them one by one; each named person's shadow peels toward the fields. Lior interrupts the count, shouting his full name and claiming the tithe entire. Beat: climax ignites—one man choosing to be seen after a lifetime of hiding.

chapters.title: Answering Questions
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, dreamlike confrontation. The entity asks him the questions it asked his mother: what he fears, whom he loves, what he'd trade. Answering honestly, he discovers truth itself disrupts the count—a bargain requires lies, and he refuses to lie anymore. Beat: the thematic turn; loyalty and truth reconciled.

chapters.title: The Tithe Refused
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The family refuses to let Lior go alone; Wren speaks all their names together, binding the count to a household that chooses itself rather than surrendering members. The bell cracks mid-toll. The entity, denied both sacrifice and division, unravels into the harvested field. Beat: climax resolved through solidarity, not substitution.

chapters.title: After the Moon
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Dawn: the fingerprints gone, the recordings silent, the bell still. Lior burns the tapes in the yard while the family watches. Marek asks him to stay for breakfast—not as a contractor. Beat: exhaustion, release, the fragile first morning of a new shape of family.

chapters.title: Counted
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, epilogue. Months later, Lior keeps the farmhouse keys on his ring and answers when they call. At night he sometimes hears a faint counting far off—and whispers 'four' back, correcting it, keeping them safe by refusing to be uncounted. Final beat: peace earned, vigilance kept, belonging chosen.
